requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: Each entry in the DNSxL MUST have an A record.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: DNSBLs SHOULD have a TXT record that describes the reason for the entry.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: DNSWLs MAY have a TXT record that describes the reason for the entry.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: The contents of the A record MUST NOT be used as an IP address.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: The A record contents conventionally have the value 127.0.0.2, but MAY have other values as described below in Section 2.3.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: Client software MUST check the A record and MAY check the TXT record.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: If a range of addresses is listed in the DNSxL, the DNSxL MUST contain an A record (or a pair of A and TXT records) for every address in the DNSxL.

requirements.heading: IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: Conversely, if an IP address is not listed in the DNSxL, there MUST NOT be any records for the address.

requirements.heading: Combined IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: DNSxLs with sublists SHOULD use both subdomains and one of the other methods.

requirements.heading: Combined IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: If a DNSxL contains both entries for a main domain and for sublists, sublist names MUST be at least two characters and contain non-digits, so there is no problem of name collisions with entries in the main domain, where the IP addresses consist of digits or single hex characters.

requirements.heading: Combined IP Address DNSxL
requirements.text: There is no widely used convention for mapping sublist names to bits or values, beyond the convention that all A values SHOULD be in the 127.0.0.0/8 range to prevent unwanted network traffic if the value is erroneously used as an IP address.

requirements.heading: IPv6 DNSxLs
requirements.text: Each entry's name MUST be a 32-component hex nibble-reversed IPv6 address suffixed by the DNSxL domain.

requirements.heading: Domain Name DNSxLs
requirements.text: The names of their entries MUST contain the listed domain name followed by the name of the DNSxL.

requirements.heading: DNSxL Cache Behavior
requirements.text: The Time to Live (TTL) and refresh times SHOULD be chosen to reflect the expected rate of change of the DNSxL.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: IPv4-based DNSxLs MUST contain an entry for 127.0.0.2 for testing purposes.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: IPv4-based DNSxLs MUST NOT contain an entry for 127.0.0.1.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: DNSBLs that return multiple values SHOULD have multiple test addresses so that, for example, a DNSBL that can return 127.0.0.5 would have a test record for 127.0.0.5 that returns an A record with the value 127.0.0.5, and a corresponding TXT record.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: IPv6-based DNSxLs MUST contain an entry for ::FFFF:7F00:2 (::FFFF: 127.0.0.2), and MUST NOT contain an entry for ::FFFF:7F00:1 (::FFFF: 127.0.0.1), the IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Address [RFC4291] equivalents of the IPv4 test addresses.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: Domain-name-based DNSxLs MUST contain an entry for the [RFC2606] reserved domain name "TEST" and MUST NOT contain an entry for the reserved domain name "INVALID".

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: DNSxLs also MAY contain A and/or AAAA records at the apex of the DNSxL zone that point to a web server, so that anyone wishing to learn about the bad.example.net DNSBL can check http://bad.example.net.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: The combination of a test address that MUST exist and an address that MUST NOT exist allows a client system to check that a domain still contains DNSxL data, and to defend against DNSxLs that deliberately or by accident install a wildcard that returns an A record for all queries.

requirements.heading: Test and Contact Addresses
requirements.text: DNSxL clients SHOULD periodically check appropriate test entries to ensure that the DNSxLs they are using are still operating.

requirements.heading: Typical Usage of DNSBLs and DNSWLs
requirements.text: If a /24 or larger range of addresses is listed, and the zone's server uses traditional zone files to represent the DNSxL, the DNSxL MAY use wildcards to limit the size of the zone file.

requirements.heading: Typical Usage of DNSBLs and DNSWLs
requirements.text: A client MUST interpret any returned A record as meaning that an address or domain is listed in a DNSxL.

requirements.heading: Typical Usage of DNSBLs and DNSWLs
requirements.text: DNSxL clients SHOULD be able to use bit masks and value range tests on returned A record values in order to select particular sublists of a combined list.

requirements.heading: Typical Usage of DNSBLs and DNSWLs
requirements.text: Long-running mail servers MAY cache DNSxL data internally, but MUST respect the TTL values and discard expired records.

requirements.heading: Typical Usage of DNSBLs and DNSWLs
requirements.text: Packages that test multiple header fields MUST be able to distinguish among values in lists with sublists because, for example, an entry indicating that an IP address is assigned to dialup users might be treated as a strong indication that a message would be rejected if the IP address sends mail directly to the recipient system, but not if the message were relayed through an ISP's mail server.

requirements.heading: Security Considerations
requirements.text: Any system manager that uses DNSxLs is entrusting part of his or her server management to the parties that run the lists, and SHOULD ensure that the management policies for the lists are consistent with the policies the system manager intends to use.

requirements.heading: Security Considerations
requirements.text: To avoid this situation, systems that use DNSxLs SHOULD check for the test entries described in Section 5 to ensure that a domain actually has the structure of a DNSxL, and SHOULD NOT use any DNSxL domain that does not have correct test entries.
